title: Trump: Mogilevich & BNY caught in largest money-laundering scheme in U.S. history
description_short: Trump: Mogilevich & BNY caught in largest money-laundering scheme in U.S. history
description_medium: In August 1999, investigators examined billions of dollars transferred from Russia through Bank of New York accounts. Some accounts were believed to be connected to Russian businessman Semion Mogilevich, whom investigators described as an organized-crime figure. The case raised questions about the source of the funds and the bank’s controls for detecting suspicious transfers. It predates Trump’s presidency.
description_long: In August 1999, investigators examined billions of dollars that had moved from Russia through accounts at the Bank of New York. Some accounts were believed to be linked to Semion Mogilevich, a Russian businessman whom investigators described as an organized-crime figure. The inquiry raised questions about the origin of the funds, the bank’s safeguards for detecting suspicious transfers, and whether bank employees had adequately scrutinized transactions. Investigators had not yet resolved the bank’s knowledge or the full source of the money when the case became public. The large sums and suspected connections made the matter a major financial-crime investigation. Allegations about the accounts were not findings that the bank knowingly participated in laundering. The event occurred in 1999 and concerned Russian money moving through a U.S. bank. The supplied event record does not establish a direct connection to Donald Trump, despite its title. That gap matters for a timeline entry about Trump: the investigation can be described as a historical case, but its relevance to Trump requires additional evidence. The documented inquiry centered on the bank’s handling of transactions and the investigators’ suspicions about some account holders. Further claims about the case should be tied to evidence from that investigation.

title: Trump Commutes Roger Stone Sentence
description_medium: After longtime ally Roger Stone was convicted on seven felony counts, including witness tampering and lying to Congress, President Trump commuted his sentence. This act of clemency rewarded a crony who had protected the president during the Mueller investigation. It was a blatant subversion of the justice system.
description_long: President Donald Trump commuted Roger Stone’s sentence on July 10, 2020, after Stone had been convicted on seven felony counts, including witness tampering and lying to Congress. A commutation reduces or ends a sentence but does not erase a conviction or reverse a jury’s verdict. Stone had been sentenced to 40 months in prison in February 2020. Trump’s action came shortly before Stone was due to report to prison and while the president was criticizing the prosecution as unfair. The White House said the commutation would allow Stone to appeal without serving time during that process. Stone had been a longtime Trump associate and a figure in the investigation of Russian interference in the 2016 election. The decision drew criticism because the president granted relief to a political ally whose case involved efforts to mislead Congress and obstruct an investigation tied to his campaign. Those concerns were about favoritism and accountability; they do not alter the formal effect of the clemency. Stone’s convictions remained in place after the sentence was commuted. The event therefore records executive intervention on behalf of an ally, not an acquittal or finding that the criminal case had been invalid.

title: Trump Truth Social Post Before Tariff Pause: 'THIS IS A GREAT TIME TO BUY!!!'
description_short: Trump Truth Social Post Before Tariff Pause: 'THIS IS A GREAT TIME TO BUY!!!'
description_medium: Shortly before announcing the 90-day tariff pause on April 9, 2025, Trump posted on Truth Social that 'THIS IS A GREAT TIME TO BUY!!!' — a post that appeared to foreshadow the imminent policy reversal that sent stocks surging. The timing raised immediate and serious allegations of insider trading and market manipulation by a sitting president. Congressional Democrats and watchdog groups demanded investigations. Legal scholars noted such conduct by an ordinary citizen would constitute securities fraud.
description_long: On April 9, 2025, Donald Trump posted “THIS IS A GREAT TIME TO BUY!!! DJT” on Truth Social hours before announcing a 90-day pause in many reciprocal tariffs. The announcement prompted a sharp market rally, and the timing of the post led lawmakers and watchdog groups to call for investigation. The post was public; it did not reveal that Trump or anyone else had traded on confidential information or profited from the policy change. The sequence attracted scrutiny because the president’s tariff decisions could move stock prices, and investors had experienced a steep market decline during the preceding days. The White House denied wrongdoing. Congressional Democrats and other critics questioned whether the post, combined with the timing of the tariff announcement, raised concerns about market manipulation or insider trading. Those were calls for investigation and legal questions, not findings that Trump committed a securities offense. The post itself urged buying but did not identify a particular security beyond the “DJT” ticker reference. The event documents the timing of the social-media message, the subsequent policy announcement, and the ensuing demands for oversight. The outcome of any inquiry is a separate matter from the sequence that prompted it.

title: Trump Administration official arrested for involvement in Capitol attack
description_short: Trump Administration official arrested for involvement in Capitol attack
description_medium: Former State Department official Federico Klein was arrested on March 4, 2021, in connection with the January 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol. Klein had worked on Donald Trump's 2016 campaign and transition before serving in the department. Prosecutors accused him of assaulting police and obstructing Congress's certification proceeding. An arrest and indictment are allegations, not a conviction.
description_long: Federico “Freddie” Klein, a former State Department official who had worked on Trump’s 2016 campaign and transition, was arrested on March 4, 2021, in connection with the January 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol. Prosecutors accused him of assaulting police officers, obstructing Congress’s electoral-vote count, and interfering with officers during civil disorder. An affidavit described video in which Klein used a riot shield against doors officers were trying to hold and urged others to join the confrontation. Klein had served in the State Department’s Bureau of Western Hemisphere Affairs and held a security clearance. The arrest began criminal proceedings; it was not a conviction. Klein later pleaded guilty and was sentenced to nearly six years in prison. That later plea and sentence resolved the case after the arrest. His former government service made the prosecution notable, but did not itself establish guilt. The case formed part of the broader prosecution of people accused of attacking police and disrupting the certification of the 2020 election. The charges and later sentence concerned Klein’s actions during the Capitol assault, not his campaign work or a finding that the Trump administration directed the attack.

title: RFK Jr Holds Up $600 Million in Global Vaccine Funding Over Debunked Thimerosal Claims
description_short: RFK Jr Holds Up $600 Million in Global Vaccine Funding Over Debunked Thimerosal Claims
description_medium: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. withheld $600 million in appropriated U.S. funding for Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, which supports immunization in low-income countries. The dispute centered on thimerosal, a preservative Kennedy has linked to autism despite evidence finding no causal connection. The money faced a September 2026 expiration deadline if unused. On July 29, Reuters reported that the administration would release the funds, reversing the hold after lawmakers sought explanations.
description_long: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. held up $600 million in congressionally appropriated funding for Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, which supports immunization programs in low-income countries. The dispute centered on thimerosal, a preservative Kennedy has linked to autism; scientific evidence has not established a causal connection. Gavi’s programs included immunization work in 30 countries, and the funds were due to expire at the end of September 2026 if unused. Lawmakers sought an explanation for the hold. On July 29, 2026, Reuters reported that the administration had decided to release the $600 million, reversing the funding delay. The decision restored access to money Congress had already appropriated and allowed it to be used for the global vaccine effort. The reporting established the administration’s reversal but did not specify when each recipient received funds or how many vaccination activities had been postponed. The episode concerned the administration of an existing appropriation and the role of disputed claims about a vaccine preservative in delaying international health funding. The release changed the funds’ immediate status; any effects on particular vaccination campaigns would depend on their timing and implementation.

title: Trump threatens using military to kill Black Lives Matter protesters
description_short: Trump threatens using military to kill Black Lives Matter protesters
description_medium: Trump used a phrase linking looting with shooting in a May 29, 2020 post about unrest in Minneapolis after George Floyd's death. He also threatened to send the National Guard and criticized local leadership. Twitter placed a warning on the post for violating its rules on glorification of violence, making access subject to an additional notice.
description_long: On May 29, 2020, President Donald Trump posted about unrest in Minneapolis following the killing of George Floyd. The post linked looting with shooting and warned that he would send the National Guard if city officials did not control the situation. Twitter placed a warning on the post under its rules against glorifying violence, requiring users to open it before viewing. Trump also criticized local leadership as protests and fires continued in the city. The post became a flashpoint in debates over the president’s response to demonstrations and the platform’s moderation of political speech. Its language was widely read as threatening, though it did not identify a specific unit or direct an order to shoot protesters. The warning limited the post’s immediate display on Twitter but did not remove it. Minneapolis was dealing with demonstrations, property damage, and public anger after Floyd’s death, while officials were responding to unrest and calls for accountability. The episode documents the president’s public threat of federal force, his criticism of city officials, and the platform’s decision to add a warning. It does not establish that the post itself caused a particular act of violence or that all protesters were involved in looting.

preserved_fields.description_short: Trump threatens using military to kill Black Lives Matter protesters

notes: Twitter added a warning to the May 29, 2020 post under its violence-related rules. The post did not name a specific unit or order troops to shoot protesters.

title: Trump advisor Peter Navarro releases report claiming rampant voter fraud
description_short: Trump advisor Peter Navarro releases report claiming rampant voter fraud
description_medium: White House trade adviser Peter Navarro published a 36-page report on December 17, 2020, alleging six categories of irregularities in the presidential election. The report cited changes in vote totals as mail ballots were counted and events at a Georgia counting site. Election officials and courts had already rejected or disputed major claims in the report. Its publication amplified efforts to challenge Joe Biden's victory but did not establish that the election was fraudulent.
description_long: White House trade adviser Peter Navarro released a 36-page report on December 17, 2020, alleging six categories of irregularities in the presidential election. The document cited changing vote leads as states counted mail ballots, footage from an Atlanta ballot-counting site, and allegations about Detroit. State and local election officials disputed key claims, and courts had rejected several related challenges. The report was not an official audit or a judicial finding. It presented Navarro’s argument for contesting the result as Trump and his allies pressed states and Congress to reject certified outcomes. The election-night leads changed as different kinds of ballots were counted; that sequence was not evidence by itself of fraud. Georgia officials disputed the report’s interpretation of the Atlanta footage, and a judge criticized claims concerning Detroit. Joe Biden’s victory had been certified by the states before Navarro released the report. The document added a formal presentation from a senior administration adviser to the broader post-election campaign to challenge the result. Its publication amplified allegations but did not prove that widespread fraud had changed the outcome. The distinction between claims in a report and findings established through audits, officials, or courts is central to understanding its significance.

title: Trump Left the Door Open to Sending Ground Troops Into Iran
description_short: Trump Left the Door Open to Sending Ground Troops Into Iran
description_medium: Trump left the door open to sending U.S. ground troops into Iran, which is the sort of phrase presidents use right before pretending everyone else misunderstood them. The significance is not just military; it reveals how casually he treats escalation ladders that would cost other people their bodies, homes, and futures. Once a president says it on camera, the Overton window shifts and the war machine hears permission.
description_long: On March 16, 2026, President Donald Trump declined to rule out sending U.S. ground troops into Iran. The remarks kept a direct ground operation among the publicly discussed options during the conflict. PBS NewsHour reported the statement, while NBC News separately reported that the administration was weighing options involving U.S. troops inside Iran. The reports did not describe an invasion order or establish that a deployment had begun. The distinction matters because a refusal to rule out an option signals that it remains under consideration, while a decision to deploy forces would require further action. Ground troops would expose U.S. service members to direct combat and could expand the scope of the conflict beyond air or naval operations. The public remarks also gave allies, adversaries, and Congress a basis to assess the administration’s stated posture. At the time, the specific mission, scale, timing, and objectives of any possible ground deployment were not stated in the cited coverage. The event is Trump’s public openness to the option and contemporaneous reporting that officials were weighing troop scenarios. It is not evidence that an invasion had been ordered or that U.S. forces had entered Iran.

title: Trump Pardons 1500 January 6 Rioters Including 600 Who Assaulted Police Officers
description_short: Trump Pardons 1500 January 6 Rioters Including 600 Who Assaulted Police Officers
description_medium: On his first day back in office January 20, 2025, Trump pardoned or commuted sentences for all 1500 people charged in connection with the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack, including over 600 convicted of assaulting, resisting, or interfering with police officers. Pardoned rioters immediately returned to the Capitol on the fifth anniversary of the attack. As of January 2026, at least 33 of those pardoned had been charged with or convicted of new crimes.
description_long: On January 20, 2025, Trump issued sweeping clemency for people prosecuted over the January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol. The action covered more than 1,500 defendants through pardons and commutations, including over 600 people convicted of assaulting, resisting, or interfering with police. A pardon forgives a federal offense, while a commutation reduces or ends a sentence; the two forms of relief have different legal effects. Trump’s order also directed dismissal of pending cases. The clemency ended or reduced the federal penalties imposed after the attack, which disrupted Congress’s certification of the 2020 election. It prompted debate about accountability, the pardon power, and the treatment of violence against law enforcement and the electoral process. Some recipients later faced new charges, but subsequent allegations do not establish that the clemency caused later conduct. The decision applied broadly to the January 6 prosecutions rather than being limited to a small set of individualized petitions. Its reach included people convicted of serious assaults as well as defendants charged with other offenses. The event marks a major reversal of the federal government’s prosecution effort and a consequential use of presidential clemency.

title: Trump Posts Threatening Image of Himself with Baseball Bat Next to DA Bragg Photo
description_short: Trump Posts Threatening Image of Himself with Baseball Bat Next to DA Bragg Photo

Bragg was investigating hush-money payments connected to the 2016 campaign. The post drew criticism as threatening, and Bragg’s office later cited it in court filings. Legal experts and Trump supporters offered competing interpretations; no court finding described the image itself as witness intimidation.
description_long: In March 2023, Donald Trump posted an image on Truth Social showing himself holding a baseball bat beside a photograph of Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg. Bragg was then overseeing an investigation into hush-money payments connected to the 2016 campaign. The juxtaposition drew criticism as threatening, although the post did not explicitly state an intent to harm Bragg. Bragg’s office later cited the image in court filings as part of a broader account of Trump’s public conduct toward prosecutors and witnesses. Some legal observers said the image could be viewed as an attempt to intimidate, while Trump’s supporters argued it was political expression. Those were competing interpretations; the cited reporting did not identify a court finding that this image itself constituted witness intimidation. Its timing mattered because it appeared during an active criminal investigation of Trump. The post contributed to concerns about pressure directed at public officials carrying out legal duties, while questions of intent and legal effect remained unresolved. The incident documents the image, its context, and the reactions it generated. It should not be treated as proof that Bragg or a witness was physically threatened, or as a judicial determination of criminal conduct.
